rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between an angle and an assertion. Its line, "no enterprise sales team mentioned for this launch," preserves the hole and turns it into proof work; B's headline, "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team," walks straight past the fact block and starts freelancing. Same three broad shapes, but A is the one a founder could hand to PR without first disinfecting the overclaims.
gaps_in_A: "which incumbent tools Linear expects PMs to leave" is the right proof ask, but the update gives no named incumbent set, so this must stay a question until Linear names the fight.

The set has no true customer/data angle because the update withholds exact count, named users, pricing, and adoption evidence. A handles that honestly, but it still leaves every kept angle dependent on follow-up proof.
gaps_in_B: "Linear is selling to the enterprise without an enterprise sales team" is overclaimed. The update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned; it does not say Linear is selling to enterprise or definitely lacks one.
"the desk that tracks Jira, Asana, Notion, and Monday" imports named competitors the update did not provide. Category context is useful; invented competitive framing is how pitches get embarrassed.
"the slower, more visual, more collaborative way non-engineers work" is a plausible thesis, not a supplied fact. It needs customer or product evidence before it can carry the design angle.

"newsjack-detector could surface a current PM-tooling or PLG-vs-sales story" is a risky extra step for this update. The launch is already the peg; do not go hunting for a fake hook unless the real one cannot carry.
